extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, fact-checkers, and researchers interested in misinformation, education controversies, and culture-war narratives
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article summarizing the origin, spread, debunking, and impacts of the 'litter boxes in schools' urban-legend/hoax across countries and political contexts. It compiles timelines, official responses, fact-checks, and related commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of credible evidence / corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checkers did not find credible news reports or verifiable evidence to support claims that schools were officially providing litter boxes for students identifying as animals or cats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no credible reports, documentation, or corroborating sources exist, the claim should be rated false (examples: Snopes rated the Michigan claim 'false'; PolitiFact found no credible reports and rated it 'Pants on Fire!'; Reuters concluded there was no evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Official school or district denials
rubrics_metrics.description: Local school boards, superintendents, and district administrators routinely issued statements denying that litter boxes or similar accommodations had been provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An authoritative denial from the named school/district (public statements, press releases, board minutes) is a primary indicator that the alleged practice did not occur; investigators should request and check official statements when evaluating such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify satirical or fabricated origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Some viral instances originated from satirical posts, fake emails, or prank videos that were taken as factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the provenance of the post or email (original account, context, satire labels). If a source is satirical or fabricated (e.g., known satire sites or admitted fake posts), treat the viral claim as false and note the source type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate emergency/preparedness uses from accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a verified, unrelated instance where cat litter appeared in classrooms as part of 'go buckets' for emergency (lockdown) toilet use, not as an accommodation for students identifying as animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about 'litter boxes in schools', check whether cited examples refer to emergency preparedness supplies or actual policy/accommodation; conflating the two is a common misinformation tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of corroboration despite political amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile repetition by politicians, media personalities, and influencers occurred frequently, but amplification did not provide verification of the underlying factual claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat political or media repetition as amplification, not evidence. Investigators should still require independent verification (documents, official confirmation, credible reporting) before treating an amplified claim as true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking outcomes and rating conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checking organizations applied explicit verdicts (e.g., 'false', 'Pants on Fire!', 'baseless') after investigation, based on evidence absence and official refutations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established fact-check ratings as indicators of investigative conclusions but review the underlying reasons (lack of evidence, denials, source provenance) to understand how the rating was reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern recognition: urban-legend / moral-panic indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Folklorists and commentators noted the hoax follows historical patterns of urban legends and moral panics (e.g., long-standing jokes about furries, generational culture-war anxieties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate new viral claims against known patterns of urban legends and moral panic dynamics (repetition, lack of verifiable evidence, targeting of marginalized groups) to assess likelihood of hoax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of motive and harm (political/transphobic intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hoax was circulated in contexts that appear aimed at discrediting LGBTQ+ and transgender accommodations, and commentators identified transphobic or political motives behind spreading the rumor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing such claims, consider the political context and potential intent to stigmatize groups; evidence of targeted messaging or alignment with anti-LGBTQ agendas is relevant to understanding why the rumor spread and its harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace amplification sources (influencers/accounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific social-media accounts and influencers (e.g., Libs of TikTok) and talk-show hosts were key nodes in spreading the rumor widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track who amplified the claim, when, and how; identifying central amplifiers helps distinguish origin, measure spread, and establish whether amplification outpaced verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and legislative response scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators and local officials sometimes proposed or considered policies (e.g., banning animal-like behavior in schools) that were motivated by or referenced the hoax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize policy proposals citing viral claims: verify the factual basis before using such claims to justify legislation; distinguish policymaking grounded in evidence from policymaking motivated by misinformation.
